# Install Python

After this page you will have a **Python 3.14** program on your computer that *you* installed, and you will know how to ask it its version.

Python itself is a program. When you type `python` (or `uv run python`), the operating system starts that program. It reads your code and carries it out. The usual implementation is **CPython** — that is what this book means by “Python” unless a page says otherwise.

## Mental model

```text
  uv (recommended)
    → downloads CPython 3.14
    → later: creates a private environment per project
    → later: installs third-party packages into that environment

  Alternatives
    → python.org installer
    → OS package (often older; fine to check “is Python here?”)
```

A **terminal** is the text window where you type commands and press Enter. On macOS it is Terminal (or iTerm). On Windows it is PowerShell or Windows Terminal. On Linux it is your distribution’s terminal. This book’s commands are meant to be typed there.

This book’s default tool is **`uv`**. One tool installs interpreters, creates isolated environments, and locks dependencies.

## Recommended: uv

Install uv with the official installer.

**Linux / macOS:**

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Close the terminal and open a new one (so `PATH` picks up the new program), then:

```bash
uv --version
```

You want a line like `uv 0.x.x`. If the command is “not found,” the installer printed a directory to add to `PATH` — the list of folders your terminal searches for programs. Follow that hint, then try `uv --version` again.

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
winget install Astral.uv
```

Or see the [uv install docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/). Open a **new** terminal after installing.

Then get Python 3.14 and check it:

```bash
uv python install 3.14
uv python list
uv run python -V
```

You want a line that starts with `Python 3.14`.

### Worked example: a throwaway lab folder

Create a folder so later chapters have a place to live. `mkdir` makes a directory; `cd` moves into it.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/src/py-lab
cd ~/src/py-lab
uv init --python 3.14
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"
```

On Windows PowerShell, `~/src/py-lab` is usually `C:\Users\YourName\src\py-lab`. Create that folder in Explorer if you prefer, then `cd` into it.

`uv init` writes a `pyproject.toml` (project metadata) and a `.python-version` file. From this directory, `uv run python` is **your** interpreter — not a random `python` that happens to be on the system.

Expected kind of output:

```text
3.14.x (main, …)
```

## Official installer (if you cannot use uv yet)

Use [python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/). On the installer, enable **Add Python to PATH** if you see that box.

On Debian/Ubuntu you can also install the OS package. It may not be 3.14 — check:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
python3 -V
```

If the OS Python is 3.12 or 3.13, you can still follow Path A. Features that need 3.14 will say so.

## Verify more than the version

```bash
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.implementation.name)"
```

| Field | Healthy result |
|-------|----------------|
| Version | `3.14.x` (or 3.12+ if you are stuck) |
| `sys.executable` | A path *you* recognize (uv cache or project `.venv`), not a mystery copy |
| Implementation | `cpython` |

`sys.executable` is the full path to the Python program that is running. If it surprises you, you are probably not in the environment you think you are.

## Windows notes

Prefer `winget install Astral.uv` or the python.org installer, then the same `uv python install 3.14` flow.

Windows sometimes has a **Store stub**: typing `python` opens the Microsoft Store instead of running Python. If that happens, use `py -3.14` or always `uv run python` from your project folder.

## What not to do

- Do not `sudo pip install` into the OS Python. That mixes your work with the system’s own tools and is hard to undo.
- Do not use Python 2. Anything that says `print "hello"` (no parentheses) is an artifact.
- Do not fight conda *and* uv in the same directory until you know why you need conda.

## What “isolated environment” will mean next

A **virtual environment** (venv) is a private copy of Python plus the packages *this* project needs. Project layout creates one. Until then, `uv run python` from `~/src/py-lab` is enough.

This page only installs the interpreter. The editor setup is the **next chapter**, not a section below.

You do not need a dozen extensions before the first `print`.

## Exercises

1. Run `uv run python -V` (or `python3 -V`) and write the exact version string in a note.
2. Print `sys.executable` and confirm you recognize the path. It is fine if it is the OS Python *only* when you chose that on purpose.
3. If `uv` is missing, install it *or* write down why you are using the OS Python for now.
